**Partior proves atomic settlement across stablecoins and tokenised deposits**

*Regulated stablecoins, tokenised deposits and digital assets can settle atomically on shared infrastructure, advancing the case for interoperable digital money in wholesale markets.*

Partior, the bank-backed global settlement platform, and digital asset infrastructure provider OpenAssets are completing a joint proof of concept demonstrating atomic delivery-versus-payment across three forms of digital money: digital assets, regulated stablecoins and commercial tokenised deposits. The test shows these instruments can settle simultaneously on a single transaction, eliminating the settlement risk that persists when legs of a trade clear at different times or on different rails.

The result lands as European and global policymakers are actively debating how different forms of tokenised money should interact. The Euro Banking Association published adoption criteria for tokenised money in June, and the BIS completed Project Aperta on cross-border open finance interoperability the same month. A working proof that stablecoins and bank-issued tokenised deposits can coexist in one settlement flow addresses a key concern for central banks and regulators weighing whether these instruments complement or compete with one another.

For wholesale market participants, atomic settlement removes the need for intermediaries to manage counterparty risk between execution and settlement. If the model scales to production, it could reshape how banks, asset managers and payment platforms approach cross-border and cross-asset transactions.

*Sources: [Partior and OpenAssets PoC proves stablecoins and tokenised deposits can settle atomically](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48180/partior-and-openassets-poc-proves-stablecoins-and-tokenised-deposits-can-settle-atomically?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**FT letter argues UK must own its payments infrastructure**

*An open banking payments firm uses the Financial Times letters page to press the case that UK payment sovereignty requires domestic ownership of core infrastructure.*

A letter published in the Financial Times argues that the UK can no longer rely on foreign-owned payments networks if it is serious about building a competitive and resilient payments market. The letter, from an open banking payments company, frames domestic ownership of infrastructure as a prerequisite for the kind of payments autonomy that policymakers have been debating with increasing urgency.

The intervention follows several months of intensifying discussion around UK payments sovereignty. The UK Payments Initiative launched in June as a domestic alternative to Visa and Mastercard, the Treasury opened a consultation on modernising payments regulation in July, and Mastercard has been exploring a sale of its Vocalink stake. Visa's €500 million European investment pledge earlier this year was itself a response to the sovereignty debate on the continent.

The letter's appearance in the FT signals that open banking firms see the current political moment as an opportunity to position account-to-account payments as a domestically owned alternative to card network dominance, not just a cheaper rail but a strategically important one.

*Sources: [Letter: UK can no longer rely on foreign-owned payments networks](https://www.ft.com/content/9fa438e5-8da7-4835-9f81-9ba1c8768ebf) — Financial Times*
stories.edited:
**TrueLayer CEO argues UK must own its payments infrastructure**

*In a letter to the Financial Times, Francesco Simoneschi presses the case that UK payment sovereignty requires domestic ownership of core infrastructure.*

In a letter to the Financial Times responding to reporting on Mastercard's potential sale of its majority stake in Vocalink, TrueLayer chief executive and co-founder Francesco Simoneschi argues that ownership of the Faster Payments operator should not simply transfer to the UK's major banks. Vocalink runs the rails that open banking payments depend on, and handing that infrastructure to an incumbent – bank or card network – would undercut the point of building a more competitive payments market, he writes.

Simoneschi sets the sale against a wider sovereignty debate, arguing that UK businesses pay billions in fees each year to Visa and Mastercard, and that regulators in the UK and across Europe are increasingly scrutinising dependence on foreign-owned card networks. A sale to the major banks would settle the sovereignty question, he writes, but not the competition one – the institutions that benefit most from the status quo would retain little incentive to change it. His preferred outcome is ownership by a coalition of independent, innovation-led challengers with a stake in opening the market up.

The letter is addressed pointedly at the Bank of England, which is shaping the next generation of UK payments infrastructure, urging it not to swap one dominant owner for another. It puts a challenger-side view on record ahead of a decision that will determine who controls the rails carrying both Faster Payments and the open banking activity built on top of it.

*Sources: [Letter: UK can no longer rely on foreign-owned payments networks](https://www.ft.com/content/9fa438e5-8da7-4835-9f81-9ba1c8768ebf) — Financial Times*
